title: Six grammatical cases mark a noun's role
explanation: Russian nouns (and their adjectives) change ending depending on their role in the sentence — nominative, genitive, accusative, dative, instrumental, prepositional.
example_gloss: I see a book. (книга → книгу, accusative)
bridge_note: English marks this only in pronouns (I/me, he/him) — Russian does it on every noun and its adjectives, closer in spirit to German's four cases, just with two more of them.

title: Verbs come in aspect pairs
explanation: Most Russian verbs have two versions — imperfective (ongoing, repeated, or in-progress) and perfective (completed, one-time) — rather than one verb used with different tenses.
example_native: Я писал письмо. / Я написал письмо.
example_gloss: I was writing a letter. / I wrote (finished) a letter.
bridge_note: English leans on phrasing to make this distinction ("was writing" vs "wrote") rather than a fully separate verb — Russian grammaticalizes it as two related but distinct words you have to learn as a pair.

title: No words for "a" or "the"
explanation: Russian has no articles at all — definiteness is inferred entirely from context and word order.
example_gloss: The book is on the table. (or: a book, depending on context)
bridge_note: English speakers learning Russian often keep reaching for a word that isn't there — the opposite problem of French/German, where the article is mandatory even in places English drops it.

title: Separate verbs for one-way vs. back-and-forth motion
explanation: Verbs of motion like "go" split into distinct words depending on whether the movement is a single trip in one direction or repeated/habitual/round-trip.
example_native: Я иду в школу. / Я хожу в школу.
example_gloss: I am going to school (right now). / I go to school (regularly).
bridge_note: English makes this distinction with context or extra words ("right now" vs "every day"), never with a different verb — this is a real vocabulary split English speakers have to build from scratch.

title: Grammatical gender is usually predictable from the noun's ending
explanation: Nouns are masculine, feminine, or neuter, but unlike French or German, the ending is a fairly reliable clue: consonant endings are usually masculine, -а/-я usually feminine, -о/-е usually neuter.
bridge_note: English has no grammatical gender to unlearn, but the comparison worth making is to French/German gender — where the ending usually gives no hint at all. Russian's endings do most of the guessing work for you.

title: Word order is flexible because case endings carry the grammar
explanation: Since case endings already show which noun is subject and which is object, word order is free to shift for emphasis rather than being fixed by grammar.
example_native: Книгу читает Анна. / Анна читает книгу.
example_gloss: Both mean "Anna is reading the book" — the emphasis just shifts.
bridge_note: English relies on rigid subject-verb-object order to show who's doing what to whom, so reordering a sentence changes its meaning. Russian can reorder freely because the case endings — not the position — carry that information.
